text: Anorien in summer is the green lap of the realm — the Pelennor deep in grass and grain, the hills in flower, and the White Mountains blue in the warm air.
Winter in Anorien is a country of white heights and green vales; the beacons stand ready on cold bare hills and the wind off the mountains is clean and sharp.
Rain over Anorien is a gentle grey curtain on the townlands; the fields drink, the orchards shine, and the White Mountains are a rumour in the mist.
Belegaer under winter is a vast grey engine — cold wind, marching waves, and the long dark of the Sea at the end of all lands.
Rain on the Sea is a grey union of sky and water; the horizon is lost, and the ship is a white mote in a weeping world.
Bree under winter is a huddle of lit windows behind a hedge and a gate; beyond the dikes the bare country waits, cold and patient.
In rain the village smells of wet thatch and woodsmoke; the road is a river of mud, and travellers come in sodden and glad of the fire.
A hard cold settles on Bree-land; the wells rim with ice and the east wind finds every gap in door and shutter.
The Vale of Anduin in winter is a grey country of mist and pale water; the river runs dark and the high banks stand cold and bare on either side.
Rain on the Anduin is a curtain drawn across the world; the far shore vanishes, and there is only the hiss of water falling on water.
A cold from the north rides the river-valley; it comes down the channel before dawn, and the mist along the banks is grey ice made air.
The Misty Mountains in winter are a white rampart across the world; the passes are sealed, and the peaks hold their storms like a grudge.
On the high passes the snow is a living thing — it drifts, it blinds, it buries; the mountains shut their gates and the wind walks abroad.
The cold of the high passes is thin, bright, and murderous; it numbs the hands on the rock and turns the breath to ice.
Dagorlad under winter is the bleakest face of the world — frost on the slag, ice on the meres, and the dead lights burning cold over the frozen pools.
The cold of Dagorlad is an unnatural cold, the cold of the marsh and the grave; it does not come with the wind so much as rise from the ground.
In heat the plain reeks and shimmers; the pits breathe out their fumes, and the very air over Dagorlad is a slow poison under the red sun.
Dale under winter is a white valley beneath a white Mountain; the river runs dark between ice-rimmed banks, and the old desolation is buried clean.
Snow on Dale hides the old scars; the valley is a white sea around the grey island of the Mountain, and the raven-call is the only sound.
The cold of Dale is the Mountain's breath — it comes down off the high snows and pools in the valley, and the raven-guards huddle on their ridge.
Drúadan in winter is a dark pine-silence under the mountain — frost in the moss, rime on the old carved stones, and the unseen folk keeping their watch.
Rain in the Drúadan is a long soft hiss in the pine-tops and a black drip below; the forest drinks and says nothing.
Dunland in winter is a stern and empty country — brown hills, thin smoke, and the white wall of the mountains closing the west.
Rain over Dunland is a grey ocean of water sweeping the downs; the Isen roars, the fords drown, and the hills stand black and dripping.
The cold comes out of the Gap with the west wind; it is the mountains' breath on Dunland's bare hills, and it spares no one.
Winter on the Blue Mountains is the Sea's winter — grey water, white ridges, and a wind that has come a thousand miles over the waves.
Rain on Lindon is the Sea sent over the mountains — long grey veils, dripping woods, and the white road to the Havens running wet.
The cold here is a salt cold off the Sea; it fills the gulf and climbs the blue slopes, and the ships at the Havens tug at their moorings in the ice-wind.
Eregion in winter is Hollin naked — holly dark against the snow, red berries like drops of blood, and the mountain wall closing the east.
Snow lies long in Eregion; it fills the hollows of the old road and crowns every ridge, and the high peaks burn white against the sky.
The cold of Eregion is a mountain cold, thin and bright; it comes down off the snows and the empty land rings with it.
Esgaroth under winter is a grey lake in a white land — black water, white shores, and the wooden town huddled on its piles in the ice-wind.
Rain on the Long Lake is a grey hammering on water and wood; the lake rises, the piers stream, and the mountains are ghosts.
The cold comes off the lake and into the bones; the wooden ways are slick with ice and the water is the colour of old iron.
Fangorn under winter sleeps with its eyes open — snow on the eaves, stillness under the boughs, and the slow thought of the shepherds moving in the deep wood.
In summer Fangorn is a green and golden heart, warm and vast; the light falls through the boughs like a memory of the Elder Days.
Rain on Fangorn is the forest drinking — a soft hiss on the eaves and a deep smell of wet leaves rising to meet it.
Northern Ithilien in winter is a pale country at the edge of the Shadow — frost on the broken towers, ice in the Morgul's steam, and the red sky beyond the pass.
A cold that is not all of winter hangs about the Vale; it breathes off the poisoned stream and climbs the stairs on silent feet.
Ithilien in summer is a garden gone half-wild — gold gorse, sweet herbs, and green glades under a warm sun, with the shadowed mountains always at the edge of sight.
Winter strips Ithilien to grey heath and dark wood; it is still fair, but a fair thing sleeping under frost, with the East waiting beyond the river.
Rain on Ithilien is soft and fragrant; it beads the gorse, quickens the herbs, and washes the smoke of the East from the clean northern air.
Lamedon in winter is a green vale gone grey — snow on the high fields, lights early in the windows, and the Blackroot running loud under its cold banks.
Snow wraps the upper vale and the feet of the White Mountains; the Morthond runs black between white banks, and the Dimholt is a dark mouth in the white.
The cold of Lamedon is a mountain cold sharpened by old dread — it pours off the high snows and stops at the black eaves of the Dimholt.
The Lone-lands under rain are a drowned and echoing wilderness — every hollow a stream and every stream in spate.
Winter strips the Lone-lands to bone — frozen heath, pale grass, and the empty track of the Road running on to horizons without a light.
The cold here is a great emptiness made palpable; it comes with the wind off the downs and stays long after the wind has gone.
Winter cannot enter the heart of Lórien — beyond the Silverlode the wind may bite, but under the mallorns the gold leaves hold an older season.
Lórien in high summer is the world's own golden afternoon — light held in leaves, song on the water, and time gone slow.
Rain in Lórien is a soft grey blessing; it passes, and the leaves shine brighter than gold beneath the washed sky.
Mirkwood in winter is a black-and-white maze — bare black boughs, grey light, and the dim paths hidden under frost and dead leaves.
Summer in Mirkwood is a stifling green dark; the heat stands still under the canopy and the forest breathes slowly in its sleep.
Rain on Mirkwood is a long black dripping; the eaves shed it for days and the paths run with dark water.
The Woodland Realm in winter is a green court gone white — bare beeches, the river dark and cold, and the warm halls hidden under the hill.
Summer under the Elvenking's eaves is a green and golden twilight — feasts in the glades, lanterns among the leaves, and the river running dark below.
Rain on the north-wood is soft and long; the beech-woods drip, the river rises, and the doors of the halls stand open to the wet dark.
Moria's gates in winter face a white and hollow land; the Dimrill Dale is drifted deep, and the old road is a rumour under the snow.
Snow falls on Moria's hidden doors as it fell when the doors were open; the mountain keeps its secrets equally under white or stone.
The cold about the West-gate is the cold of deep places — it seeps up out of the earth as much as it blows down from the peaks.
Heat rules the plateau — the air is a kiln-breath through the fumes, the stone burns the foot, and the only water is warm and bitter.
Cold in Mordor is a knife in a sheath of fumes — it waits in the ravines and the shadows of the walls, and at night the plain gives up its heat and freezes.
Winter turns Gorgoroth from furnace to forge-cold; the ash is bound by black frost, and the red sky hangs low over the frozen pits.
The Anduin vales under winter are a quiet land of black water and white hills; the fords freeze at their edges and the mountains close in.
Snow on the vales makes a clean and silent world — white meadows, black water, and the dark line of the forest under its burden.
Rain brings the mountain-streams down and the Anduin up; the fords deepen, the fens spread, and the valley fills with the sound of water.
Winter in the northern mountains is a season of white walls and shut passes; the goblins come and go under the snow, and the eagles watch.
Snow lies on the northern Misty Mountains from autumn to spring; the peaks are ramparts of it, and the high paths are trenches through it.
The cold in these heights is of the old, hard kind — it lives in the stone of the passes and waits for the traveller at every cave-mouth.
In winter the Old Forest is grey and bare but no less watchful; the willows sleep lightly, and the paths belong to them alone.
The Old Forest under rain is a green darkness full of small sounds — drip and trickle and the creak of wet wood. Nothing hurries; the rain is the Forest's own.
The Field of Celebrant lies open to the winter wind; the old defeat is only a greener line in the dead grass, and the mountains are white and near.
In summer the field is a green and golden sea; the larks are up, and the old scars are hidden in flower and leaf.
The cold rides down off the mountains and across the open field; there is no shelter on the grass, and the sky is pale iron.
Rivendell in winter is a green heart in a grey land — frost and wind on the high moors, and warm light and falling water in the sheltered vale.
Rain comes down the valley soft and cold; the Bruinen rises, the mountains vanish in mist, and Rivendell is shut away behind a curtain of silver.
Summer lingers in Rivendell beyond its season — warm air on the terraces, long light in the leaves, and the sound of water falling into evening.
The Mark under winter is a sea of grey grass under a white wall; the wind is the lord of it, and the land rings hollow under the hooves.
Rohan in high summer is a green sea of grass and wind; the larks are up, the horses are sleek, and the mountains stand blue and far.
Cold on the Mark is a wind-cold, endless and searching; it has the whole width of the plain to gather in, and it comes like a spear.
The lake-country in winter is a stern land — dark water, white-crowned peaks about the falls, and the sound of Rauros rolling through the cold.
Rain over the long lake is a grey world of falling water and rising mist; the Falls thunder unseen behind the curtain.
A keen cold comes down the ravines of the Emyn Muil; it carries the smell of the dead meres and leaves the stones ringing.
The Shire in summer is all abundance — laden orchards, humming bees, fields high with hay, and long warm evenings over the Water.
Under winter the Shire turns quiet — frost on the thatch, snow along the lanes, and warm light in the windows behind the hedgerows.
Rain comes softly and often here; it silvers the hedges, fills the streams, and beads the long grass. The land looks washed and grateful.
Winter on the Tower Hills is a green land gone grey at the edge of the Sea — bare woods, white towers, and the smell of the salt wind.
Rain over the Tower Hills comes off the Sea; it beats on the white towers and runs down the green slopes to the road that ends at the world's edge.
The Trollshaws in rain are a sodden cheerless maze of hills — soaked woods, rising fords, and no dry ground under heaven.
Winter locks the Trollshaws fast — black rock, white ravines, and the growl of streams half-frozen in their beds.
The cold gathers in the folds of the Trollshaws and stays; the caves breathe it and the paths are fangs of ice.
The Weather Hills in rain are a sodden secret country — grey ridges in streaming mist, with water running in every crevice of the old stones.
Winter lays the hills bare — iron grass, black thorn, and the empty crowns of the watch-towers against a colourless sky.
A searching cold owns these hills; it pours down the lee slopes at night and pools in the hollows till dawn.
The Wold in winter is the loneliest part of the Mark — white downs, black thorn-brakes, and the far dark of Fangorn like a wall between worlds.
Cold on the Wold is a northern cold; it comes down the vale of the Anduin and across the empty downs, and there is no hill to hide behind.
The Woodmen's country in winter is a white-drifted forest of black oaks; the halls are warm behind their stockades and the deer-yards are silent.
Summer in the Beornings' woodland is green gold — oak-shade, high meadows, and honey in the hollow trees.
